title: Dating Deep Time: From Steno to Patterson
learningObjectives: Order major advances in geologic time thinking from 1669 to 1956 on a timeline.
Explain how superposition and faunal succession established relative order before absolute dating.
Describe how radioactivity and lead-lead dating revised Earth's age to about 4.55 billion years.

explanations.text: Early geologists established relative time by ordering rock layers and fossils before they could measure absolute ages.

evidence.quote: In 1788, James Hutton proposed what would become the foundational principle of geology — uniformitarianism.
no vestige of a beginning. No prospect of an end.

explanations.text: Hutton argued that slow processes seen today shaped Earth in the past, implying vast geologic time.

evidence.quote: It was the discovery of radioactivity in 1896 that changed the heat-flow picture dramatically.
It was 1956 when Clair Cameron Patterson, an American geochemist, used lead-lead dating

explanations.text: Discovery of radioactivity provided heat to explain long time and tools to date rocks, leading to Patterson's Earth age.

evidence.quote: Nicholas Steno, 1669, gets credit for first writing down basic geological principles as laws.
The law of superposition says that older rocks are on the bottom and younger rocks are on the top.
In 1788, James Hutton proposed what would become the foundational principle of geology — uniformitarianism.
In 1815, Smith developed the law of faunal succession
species become extinct and are replaced by new species
The first geologic time scale was published in 1841 — Powell certainly would have known of it and used it in his geologic trips to the West.
It was the discovery of radioactivity in 1896 that changed the heat-flow picture dramatically.
English geologist Arthur Holmes in 1913 calculated an age of 1.6 billion years
the first such estimate based on radiometric dating

this date was accepted as the age of Earth
